| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P001 — Explicit decision owner, consumer, deadline, and action authority | Analysis begins with an owner-action-deadline tuple and ends in an implementable choice, deferment, experiment, policy, or documented non-decision. | Any consequential allocation, schedule, optimisation, trade study, forecast-controlled action, or automated policy. | For low-consequence reversible choices, name one accountable chooser and a decision time; no formal charter is required. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=LOW |
| P002 — Frame the real decision and consequence before selecting a model | Model choice is downstream of a challengeable decision frame and can be changed without changing the underlying consequence statement. | Whenever analysis will rank alternatives, allocate scarce resources, or automate action. | A one-page decision frame or direct authoritative constraint can suffice where alternatives are few and consequence is clear. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=MODERATE |
| P003 — Generate and preserve meaningful alternatives before ranking or optimisation | The decision set is treated as an engineered object with provenance, feasibility screening, dominance checks and a reopen rule. | High-consequence, irreversible, novel or underperforming decisions; decisions where all listed options score poorly. | For routine choices, screen a small known set and ask explicitly whether a materially different option exists. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=MODERATE |
| P005 — Distinguish feasible alternatives, enforceable hard constraints, and soft preferences | Constraint status is challengeable and linked to enforcement, uncertainty, recourse and violation consequence; infeasibility is diagnostic, not proof that reality is impossible. | Any optimisation, schedule, allocation or scored trade study with limits or prerequisites. | Use direct admissibility screening before scoring; a hard authoritative discriminator can end the comparison. | formal=HIGH; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=MODERATE |
| P006 — Trace objectives to consequences and resist proxy substitution | A proxy remains provisional evidence about a consequence, with independent outcome validation and an explicit gaming/feedback model. | Whenever a KPI, score, forecast loss, utilisation, throughput, service level, or learned reward controls incentives or action. | Where a direct outcome or authoritative constraint is observable, use it instead of a composite proxy. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P011 — Match model fidelity and analysis depth to decision consequence | Use the least-cost model that is adequate to discriminate the consequential decision, with a reopen rule when state or sensitivity changes. | Any choice of modelling depth, simulation detail, data collection, solver exactness or review breadth. | Use bounds, dominance, sensitivity or a simple discriminator before building a richer model. | formal=HIGH; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=MODERATE |
| P012 — Give cheap authoritative discriminators and simple heuristics precedence when sufficient | Simple rules are preferred when validated for the context and monitored for drift; complexity is justified by incremental decision value, not prestige. | Low-consequence, reversible, time-limited, repeated or structurally simple decisions, and preliminary screening of complex decisions. | This property is itself the cheap path: apply the least expensive valid discriminator with explicit limits. | formal=HIGH; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P015 — State model assumptions and validity domain as part of the decision claim | Claims are scoped: optimal/valid under a stated representation and current evidence, with explicit transfer and drift limits. | Any formal model, simulation, forecast, queue formula, scorecard, optimisation or learned policy. | List only assumptions capable of changing action; use a direct caveat and fallback when validation is infeasible. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P016 — Test sensitivity to parameters, probabilities, weights, and modelling choices | Sensitivity is tied to whether action changes, not merely to output variance; unstable decisions trigger more information, robust options or preserved alternatives. | Close rankings, uncertain coefficients, high consequence, disputed preferences, unstable forecasts or model choice ambiguity. | Use one-way break-even and dominance tests before global or probabilistic sensitivity analysis. | formal=HIGH; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P018 — Separate solver or model optimality from real-decision validity | No recommendation controls action solely because an optimiser converged; each validity layer has evidence and ownership. | Any solver-backed, simulation-optimised or learned recommendation. | State ‘optimal under this model’ and independently challenge the model with domain/authority checks. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P019 — Establish implementation feasibility, operational authority, and usable decision support | Implementation is part of model validity; resistance can be evidence of missing constraints rather than a defect in users. | Any recommendation requiring organisational behaviour, software integration, recurring operator use, or automated enforcement. | For one-off simple decisions, verify authority, resource availability and direct executability with the responsible operator. | formal=LOW; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=MODERATE |
| P021 — Represent demand, arrivals, service, capacity, and variability before capacity claims | Use the least-assumptive demand/capacity representation that discriminates overload, waiting and reserve decisions, with transient validation. | Shared service systems with stochastic demand, backlogs, latency/service commitments or capacity investment. | Measure arrivals, completions, backlog age, utilisation and peak-to-average behaviour before fitting a parametric queue. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P022 — Govern utilisation jointly with waiting, congestion, and tail performance | Efficiency is assessed at system throughput and service consequence, not maximum busy fraction; controlled idle capacity can be rational. | Variable demand, finite deadlines, latency-sensitive service, failure/retry loops or expensive queues. | Plot utilisation, queue age and tail delay together; reduce load or add reserve when congestion inflects. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P024 — Identify system bottlenecks and optimise end-to-end flow rather than local utilisation | Capacity action is justified by marginal end-to-end consequence and accounts for bottleneck migration after intervention. | Networks, pipelines, multi-stage workflows, shared tests/approvals, production/service systems and interdependent resource pools. | Compare arrival/completion rates and queue age by stage; test whether adding local capacity changes end-to-end flow. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=MODERATE |
| P025 — Size capacity reserve and slack from variability, consequence, recovery, and coupling | Reserve is a priced hedge and recovery option, not waste or virtue; it is conditional, observable and periodically recalibrated. | Consequential delay/shortage, variable or bursty demand, slow recovery, failure-prone capacity or tightly coupled stages. | Use peak/backlog/recovery observations and a bounded reserve rule before fitting a full queue/inventory model. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P029 — Schedule parallel work from real precedence, resource, and acceptance conflicts | Parallelism is authorised by current conflict evidence and recomputed after state changes; neither issue-wide serialisation nor maximal concurrency is default. | Multiple ready work units with potential dependency or resource interaction. | Topological plus resource-conflict screening and a simple list/dispatch rule. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P032 — Recompute schedules and allocations after material state change | The schedule is a current decision policy with explicit recomputation and freeze/stability rules, not an archival chart. | Task completion/failure, new work, duration overrun, resource loss, priority/constraint change or observed demand regime shift. | Re-run a simple priority/resource-conflict rule on current state instead of rebuilding a full optimisation. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P041 — Distinguish variability, parameter uncertainty, ambiguity, model-form error, and nonstationarity | The uncertainty claim states what is known, estimated, bounded, disputed or unmodelled, and does not overgeneralise protection. | Material uncertain demand, duration, cost, state transition, model class, preference or external regime. | Use separate labels and bounds; avoid assigning probabilities where identification is weak. | formal=HIGH; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=MODERATE; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P042 — Represent recourse and state-contingent corrective action | Robustness is achieved partly through credible recoverability, with recourse capacity and authority validated rather than assumed. | Multi-stage commitments, recoverable failures, adaptive staffing/scheduling, inventory replenishment or uncertain implementation. | List credible fallback actions and recovery limits; use scenario-specific rules before full stochastic programming. | formal=HIGH; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P043 — Treat tail, rare, irreversible, and high-consequence outcomes explicitly | Tail protection is matched to consequence and evidence; probabilities and confidence levels are owned assumptions, not objective facts. | Irreversible loss, catastrophic failure, strict service/safety thresholds, extreme latency or correlated disruption. | Use consequence-based worst credible case or hard threshold when probabilities are not identifiable. | formal=HIGH; empirical=MODERATE; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P050 — Verify implementation and validate simulation against its decision purpose | A simulation has a bounded credibility claim tied to a decision, state, data regime and consequence—not a certificate that the model is true. | Simulation output materially changes design, capacity, schedule, policy, safety margin, investment or resource allocation. | For low-consequence questions, use hand checks, extreme cases and comparison with observed/simple analytical behaviour. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P053 — Detect and resist objective, constraint, data, queue, and reporting gaming | Targets are treated as interventions in a socio-technical system, with protected provenance and independent consequences that can invalidate the metric. | High-stakes KPIs, allocation rules, service levels, ranked alternatives, algorithmic control, incentives or politically contested optimisation. | Use a direct outcome plus one counter-metric and inspect boundary cases/reclassifications; avoid composite scores where direct authority suffices. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |
| P055 — Monitor realised consequences and retire or revise models after drift | Validity is time-bounded and consequence-tested; a model remains authoritative only while owned evidence supports its current decision use. | Recurring or automated decisions, long-lived models, changing demand/capacity, adaptive adversaries, or high-consequence recommendations. | For one-off reversible choices, record the outcome and a bounded reopen trigger; do not establish permanent monitoring machinery. | formal=MODERATE; empirical=HIGH; field=HIGH; implementation=HIGH; transfer=HIGH; assumption_sensitivity=HIGH |

### P001 — Explicit decision owner, consumer, deadline, and action authority

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** A model, dashboard, or recommendation has no live decision consumer, no deadline, or ambiguous authority, so analysis cannot control action legitimately.

**MATURE_FORM:** Analysis begins with an owner-action-deadline tuple and ends in an implementable choice, deferment, experiment, policy, or documented non-decision.

**TRIGGER:** Any consequential allocation, schedule, optimisation, trade study, forecast-controlled action, or automated policy.

**CHEAP_PATH:** For low-consequence reversible choices, name one accountable chooser and a decision time; no formal charter is required.

**TRIGGER:** Whenever a KPI, score, forecast loss, utilisation, throughput, service level, or learned reward controls incentives or action.

### P007 — Preserve multiple objectives, Pareto structure, and non-compensatory limits

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Aggregate score improves while a critical criterion, stakeholder, tail consequence or hard threshold worsens unacceptably.

**MATURE_FORM:** Conflict remains visible; aggregation is an owned preference model, not objective truth, and alternative rankings are tested across plausible preferences.

**TRIGGER:** Decisions with genuinely conflicting consequences, stakeholder values, quality attributes or fairness/efficiency tensions.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use a small consequence table and dominance check; do not aggregate when one alternative clearly dominates or a hard threshold decides.

### P009 — Account for reversibility, irreversibility, option value, and staged commitment

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** An irreversible action is taken too early, or a reversible low-cost experiment is over-analysed as though it were final commitment.

**MATURE_FORM:** Decision depth and commitment scale are proportional to irreversibility; reversible options can be exercised cheaply while irreversible choices preserve learning value.

**TRIGGER:** Capital commitments, architecture lock-in, contracts, irreversible external actions, long-lived capacity and uncertain technology choices.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use qualitative option-preservation and reversibility screening for small or poorly quantified decisions.

  "DECISION_OWNER": "Named accountable owner",
  "INFORMATION_STATE": "Current and acquirable information",
  "IRREVERSIBILITY": "Central trigger for analysis depth",
  "MATURE_FORM": "Decision-relative framing with sensitivity and implementation authority",
  "OBJECTIVES": "Valued consequences and criteria",
  "PROPERTY": "Account for reversibility, irreversibility, option value, and staged commitment",
  "RECOVERY_OR_RECOURSE": "Rollback, pause, pilot, staged expansion, exit or no feasible recourse",
  "UNCERTAINTY": "Material uncertainty and ambiguity stated"

### P010 — Represent decision horizon, dependencies, and sequential coupling

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Myopic optimisation improves the current step while degrading future feasibility, option value, queues or total cost.

**MATURE_FORM:** The unit of decision is a state-contingent policy or staged commitment when future coupling matters, not a falsely independent one-shot optimum.

**TRIGGER:** Linked decisions, replenishment, scheduling, capacity investment, maintenance, adaptive policies and any action with material carry-over effects.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use an explicit two-step consequence/dependency check when full dynamic programming is disproportionate.

### P011 — Match model fidelity and analysis depth to decision consequence

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Analysis costs and delays grow while added fidelity cannot change the next action, or a crude model is used where small errors reverse an irreversible choice.

**MATURE_FORM:** Use the least-cost model that is adequate to discriminate the consequential decision, with a reopen rule when state or sensitivity changes.

**TRIGGER:** Any choice of modelling depth, simulation detail, data collection, solver exactness or review breadth.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use bounds, dominance, sensitivity or a simple discriminator before building a richer model.

**DECISION_FRAME_PROFILE:** NOT_PRIMARY

### P012 — Give cheap authoritative discriminators and simple heuristics precedence when sufficient

### P020 — Retire or rebuild stale models, schedules, forecasts, and metrics without a live consumer

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** A stale result retains ceremonial authority, consumes maintenance effort, or drives action outside its validity domain.

**MATURE_FORM:** Analytical authority is conditional on current state, current decision and active ownership; stale artefacts fail closed or become historical evidence only.

**TRIGGER:** Recurring dashboards, schedules, forecasts, optimisation models, simulations and decision policies.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use an explicit expiry/review date and owner; archive immediately when no live decision depends on it.

### P021 — Represent demand, arrivals, service, capacity, and variability before capacity claims

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Average capacity appears sufficient but bursts or service variability produce long queues, loss, abandonment or missed deadlines.

**MATURE_FORM:** Use the least-assumptive demand/capacity representation that discriminates overload, waiting and reserve decisions, with transient validation.

**TRIGGER:** Shared service systems with stochastic demand, backlogs, latency/service commitments or capacity investment.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Measure arrivals, completions, backlog age, utilisation and peak-to-average behaviour before fitting a parametric queue.

### P022 — Govern utilisation jointly with waiting, congestion, and tail performance

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Near-100% utilisation creates exploding delay, tail latency, abandonment, brittle recovery and hidden backlog.

**MATURE_FORM:** Efficiency is assessed at system throughput and service consequence, not maximum busy fraction; controlled idle capacity can be rational.

**TRIGGER:** Variable demand, finite deadlines, latency-sensitive service, failure/retry loops or expensive queues.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Plot utilisation, queue age and tail delay together; reduce load or add reserve when congestion inflects.

### P025 — Size capacity reserve and slack from variability, consequence, recovery, and coupling

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** System cannot absorb surge, failure, rework or recovery; or excess reserve imposes unjustified cost and hides problems.

**MATURE_FORM:** Reserve is a priced hedge and recovery option, not waste or virtue; it is conditional, observable and periodically recalibrated.

**TRIGGER:** Consequential delay/shortage, variable or bursty demand, slow recovery, failure-prone capacity or tightly coupled stages.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use peak/backlog/recovery observations and a bounded reserve rule before fitting a full queue/inventory model.

**DECISION_FRAME_PROFILE:** NOT_PRIMARY

**OBJECTIVE_CONSTRAINT_PROFILE**

### P028 — Model queue networks, shared bottlenecks, retries, rework, and blocking when coupled

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Adding capacity or parallelism at one stage worsens congestion elsewhere or increases total completion time/cost.

**MATURE_FORM:** Coupling is represented at enough fidelity to avoid local-capacity and naive-parallelism errors; exact product-form assumptions are not presumed.

**TRIGGER:** Pipelines, review/test chains, distributed services, multi-stage maintenance, workflows with rework or common dependencies.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Draw a flow/queue map and identify shared resources/retry loops before using network formulas or simulation.

### P030 — Treat resource ceilings as constraints, not utilisation targets

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Work is pulled prematurely, WIP/queues grow, option value is lost, or scarce acceptance capacity is saturated.

**MATURE_FORM:** Ceilings constrain admissible actions while utilisation remains an observed trade-off with delay, reserve and switching cost.

**TRIGGER:** Owner-supplied limits on workers, compute, money, concurrent jobs, external calls or review capacity.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Enforce the ceiling and choose the highest-value feasible ready work; do not add filler work to hit a utilisation metric.

**DECISION_FRAME_PROFILE:** NOT_PRIMARY

**OBJECTIVE_CONSTRAINT_PROFILE**

  "CHEAP_PATH": "Enforce the ceiling and choose the highest-value feasible ready work; do not add filler work to hit a utilisation metric.",

### P034 — Use work-conserving execution only within conflict, option, safety, and congestion bounds

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Starting work consumes scarce WIP/acceptance capacity, blocks higher-value arrivals, creates setup costs, destroys options or increases risk.

**TRIGGER:** Ready work exists but starting it could create shared-resource conflict, WIP, lock-in, setup, safety or priority harm.

### P035 — Value inventory, buffers, slack, and reserve conditionally rather than categorically

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Too little buffer causes shortages, coupling and recovery failure; too much creates cost, obsolescence, delay and hidden WIP.

**MATURE_FORM:** Every buffer has an owned purpose, cost, trigger, sizing basis and retirement/recalibration rule.

**TRIGGER:** Variable demand or supply, long recovery/replenishment, coupled stages, service commitments, irreversible shortages or failure recovery.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use observed stockouts/backlogs, lead time and holding/shortage asymmetry to set a bounded rule; avoid formula transfer without fit.

**DECISION_FRAME_PROFILE:** NOT_PRIMARY

### P037 — Use mathematical optimisation only when decision complexity and value warrant it

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Either needless model/solver burden or avoidable resource loss from crude manual allocation.

**MATURE_FORM:** Optimisation is a proportionate decision instrument with baseline comparison, validity evidence, sensitivity and implementability—not a badge.

**TRIGGER:** Many interacting alternatives/constraints, scarce resources, repeated decisions, non-obvious trade-offs and material payoff.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Direct feasibility/dominance test, greedy/list heuristic or small enumeration with explicit regret bound where possible.

### P041 — Distinguish variability, parameter uncertainty, ambiguity, model-form error, and nonstationarity

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** A method robust to sampled variability is claimed robust to misspecified models, structural breaks or unknown state spaces.

**MATURE_FORM:** The uncertainty claim states what is known, estimated, bounded, disputed or unmodelled, and does not overgeneralise protection.

**TRIGGER:** Material uncertain demand, duration, cost, state transition, model class, preference or external regime.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use separate labels and bounds; avoid assigning probabilities where identification is weak.

### P065 — Universal transfer of parametric queue, inventory, and scheduling formulas to knowledge or agent work remains unresolved

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_AS_UNRESOLVED_QUESTION_ONLY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** A neat M/M/1, EOQ or machine-scheduling analogy ignores strategic task selection, learning, retries, shared acceptance, endogenous service, quality variation or changing task definitions.

**MATURE_FORM:** Congestion and constraint reasoning are retained; exact formula transfer remains conditional and must be validated domain by domain.

**TRIGGER:** Novel service, software, knowledge or agentic systems where queue/capacity/schedule effects are plausible but the stochastic process is not established.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use direct WIP/backlog, elapsed-time, bottleneck and conflict observations; avoid distributional formulas until diagnostics support them.

### P066 — Use maintenance and replacement policies only with a credible failure-state and renewal model

**CROSSWALK_DISPOSITION:** CROSSWALK_WORTHY

**DECISION_OR_OPERATIONAL_FAILURE_MODE:** Premature replacement wastes capacity and parts; delayed intervention causes avoidable failure; sensor/prognostic error or common-cause dependence invalidates a nominal threshold policy.

**MATURE_FORM:** Maintenance is a state-contingent reliability-and-capacity decision whose policy is validated against actual failure behaviour, observation quality, downtime and resource coupling.

**TRIGGER:** Assets or services with material failure consequence, repeated life cycles, observable condition or age dependence, and controllable maintenance/replacement action.

**CHEAP_PATH:** Use manufacturer/field failure evidence, a conservative inspection interval, direct condition threshold or run-to-failure where consequence is low and replacement is cheap; avoid predictive optimisation without incremental value.

## CEREMONIES_TO_NOT_BLINDLY_ADOPT

- A named solver or optimisation algorithm is not a universal engineering property
- A fixed deterministic PERT/CPM/Gantt network is superseded as general schedule authority
- A universal weighted scorecard is rejected as an objective ranking mechanism
- One-hundred-percent utilisation as an efficiency target is rejected
- Simulation run count is not a general credibility property
- Universal queue/inventory formula transfer
- Giant integrated model by default
- RL/AI agent as endpoint

## CONTEXTS_WHERE_PROPERTY_SHOULD_NOT_TRIGGER

- P026: Use a transparent priority/ageing rule with explicit exceptions; avoid queueing optimisation when consequences clearly order work.
- P033: Use a minimum-improvement threshold and protect near-term committed work unless safety or feasibility changes.
- P034: Start the highest-value conflict-free work; remain idle when no eligible work has positive net consequence.
- P036: Use a policy threshold from authoritative service requirement and observed variability; do not estimate a full cost curve when not identifiable.
- P039: Check whether the incumbent and bound imply different real actions; stop if not and model uncertainty dominates.
- P040: Inspect binding constraints and perform a small finite change scenario rather than treating an infinitesimal dual as truth.
- P048: Use historical/offline evidence, a deterministic discriminator, or a small controlled pilot when full adaptive exploration is unnecessary or unsafe.
- P054: Prefer a transparent calibrated predictor plus robust/simple decision rule when end-to-end learning has no demonstrated incremental decision value.
- P062: Use a rule, bandit, rolling optimiser, supervised forecast plus policy, or human-in-the-loop decision support when these settle the operational need.
- P063: Use domain heuristics, decomposition, greedy/list scheduling or a solver with an optimality gap where sufficient.
- P065: Use direct WIP/backlog, elapsed-time, bottleneck and conflict observations; avoid distributional formulas until diagnostics support them.
- P066: Use manufacturer/field failure evidence, a conservative inspection interval, direct condition threshold or run-to-failure where consequence is low and replacement is cheap; avoid predictive optimisation without incremental value.

## OBJECTIVE_OR_PROXY_GAMING_RISKS

- Metric substitution
- Queue/backlog hiding
- Post-hoc weights or normalisation
- Constraint deletion or penalty relabelling
- Selective scenarios
- Threshold/reclassification gaming
- Cost shifting/externalities
- Decision-induced data feedback

## MODEL_MISSPECIFICATION_RISKS

- Omitted alternatives
- Invalid probability/distribution
- Unmodelled transient or common cause
- Wrong service/task abstraction
- Invalid causal intervention model
- Stale state/data
- Infeasible recourse
- Unrepresented implementation authority or switching cost

## EVOLVED_DECISION_AND_OPERATIONS_ENGINEERING_PUBLIC_DOCUMENTATION_INTAKE
## Source-grounded explanation

Operations research and management science developed as plural traditions for consequential operational choices: teletraffic and queueing studied congestion; inventory theory studied replenishment and shortage; wartime OR studied mission performance; mathematical programming formalised scarce-resource allocation; scheduling and network methods represented dependence and capacity; simulation examined complex stochastic operations; and decision analysis formalised alternatives, consequences, preferences and information value. These lineages converged, but none licenses the caricature that every problem should be handed to one optimiser. [S001–S015, S037–S041, S071–S072]

The mature engineering residue is decision-relative. It frames the real consequence and authority before modelling, generates feasible alternatives, distinguishes objectives from proxies and hard constraints from preferences, represents variability and queues before capacity claims, treats schedules as current state-dependent policies, tests sensitivity and out-of-sample consequence, validates simulation for a bounded purpose, preserves recourse and options, and stops analysis when the next result cannot change action enough to justify delay or cost. Modern stochastic, robust, data-driven and adaptive methods extend this discipline but do not remove model, calibration, implementation or governance burdens. [S020–S033, S049, S070, S084–S103]

## Strongest surviving engineering properties

| Property | Public explanation |
| --- | --- |
| P001 — Explicit decision owner, consumer, deadline, and action authority | Analysis begins with an owner-action-deadline tuple and ends in an implementable choice, deferment, experiment, policy, or documented non-decision. |
| P002 — Frame the real decision and consequence before selecting a model | Model choice is downstream of a challengeable decision frame and can be changed without changing the underlying consequence statement. |
| P003 — Generate and preserve meaningful alternatives before ranking or optimisation | The decision set is treated as an engineered object with provenance, feasibility screening, dominance checks and a reopen rule. |
| P005 — Distinguish feasible alternatives, enforceable hard constraints, and soft preferences | Constraint status is challengeable and linked to enforcement, uncertainty, recourse and violation consequence; infeasibility is diagnostic, not proof that reality is impossible. |
| P006 — Trace objectives to consequences and resist proxy substitution | A proxy remains provisional evidence about a consequence, with independent outcome validation and an explicit gaming/feedback model. |
| P011 — Match model fidelity and analysis depth to decision consequence | Use the least-cost model that is adequate to discriminate the consequential decision, with a reopen rule when state or sensitivity changes. |
| P012 — Give cheap authoritative discriminators and simple heuristics precedence when sufficient | Simple rules are preferred when validated for the context and monitored for drift; complexity is justified by incremental decision value, not prestige. |
| P015 — State model assumptions and validity domain as part of the decision claim | Claims are scoped: optimal/valid under a stated representation and current evidence, with explicit transfer and drift limits. |
| P018 — Separate solver or model optimality from real-decision validity | No recommendation controls action solely because an optimiser converged; each validity layer has evidence and ownership. |
| P021 — Represent demand, arrivals, service, capacity, and variability before capacity claims | Use the least-assumptive demand/capacity representation that discriminates overload, waiting and reserve decisions, with transient validation. |
| P022 — Govern utilisation jointly with waiting, congestion, and tail performance | Efficiency is assessed at system throughput and service consequence, not maximum busy fraction; controlled idle capacity can be rational. |
| P024 — Identify system bottlenecks and optimise end-to-end flow rather than local utilisation | Capacity action is justified by marginal end-to-end consequence and accounts for bottleneck migration after intervention. |
| P025 — Size capacity reserve and slack from variability, consequence, recovery, and coupling | Reserve is a priced hedge and recovery option, not waste or virtue; it is conditional, observable and periodically recalibrated. |
| P029 — Schedule parallel work from real precedence, resource, and acceptance conflicts | Parallelism is authorised by current conflict evidence and recomputed after state changes; neither issue-wide serialisation nor maximal concurrency is default. |
| P032 — Recompute schedules and allocations after material state change | The schedule is a current decision policy with explicit recomputation and freeze/stability rules, not an archival chart. |

## Common caricatures and ceremonies to reject

- “Operations research means optimise everything.” Historical OR was plural, empirical and decision-attached. Optimisation is warranted only after a consequential decision, feasible alternatives and valid structure exist.
- “The optimiser gives the best decision.” It gives an optimum for the represented objective, feasible set, data and assumptions. Real-decision validity, implementation and post-selection uncertainty remain separate burdens.
- “100% utilisation is efficient.” Under variability, approaching saturation can cause steep waiting and tail delay; reserve may be a congestion and recovery resource.
- “A schedule is a plan of what will happen.” A schedule is a state- and assumption-dependent allocation policy or forecast. Resource conflicts, uncertain duration and changed state require recomputation.
- “More detailed forecasts create better decisions.” Forecast detail has value only through downstream consequence; calibration, structural break, intervention feedback and decision loss can dominate point accuracy.
- “Expected value is the correct choice.” Expected value is conditional on consequence valuation and probability adequacy; tail, irreversibility, ambiguity and non-compensatory limits can require another criterion.
- “A weighted scorecard objectively ranks alternatives.” Weights, scales, independence, normalisation and compensation are value assumptions. Sensitivity or rank reversal may leave an undecided set.
- “The critical path is fixed.” Criticality depends on the current network, duration/resource state and uncertainty; resource-constrained or stochastic critical paths can change.
- “More simulation runs mean more truth.” More independent replications reduce Monte Carlo error only. They do not fix wrong inputs, transients, dependence, structural error or invalid decision use.
- “If the model is solved optimally, the engineering problem is solved.” Formulation, objective validity, externalities, uncertainty, authority, implementability and monitoring survive solver completion.

## Important criticisms and limits

- Wrong or captured objective — Local metric improves while real consequence or distribution worsens.
- Locally optimal action worsens system flow — Local utilisation, throughput or budget target shifts delay/cost to another stage.
- Near-saturation congestion collapse — High utilisation drives steep waiting and tail latency under variability.
- Steady-state queue transplanted into bursty/nonstationary work — M/M/1-style intuition fails under time variation, feedback, heavy tails or ill-defined service.
- Forecast error ignored by optimisation — Point estimates are treated as known and errors are amplified by the decision layer.
- Deterministic schedule under uncertain duration/resources — Published dates and critical path become infeasible or stale.
- PERT independence and estimate assumptions — Three-point duration aggregation underestimates correlation, merging, calendars and resource coupling.
- Weighted-score manipulation and rank reversal — Alternative, scaling, normalisation or weight changes reverse ranks.
- Expected value masks irreversible/tail consequence — Mean-optimal action violates hard consequence or creates unacceptable tail exposure.
- Robust optimisation becomes over-conservative — Protecting against implausible joint extremes destroys opportunity.

## From deterministic one-shot optimisation to uncertainty-aware adaptive decision engineering

The historical evolution is not a linear replacement story. Deterministic models remain valuable when their assumptions fit and a cheap discriminator does not suffice. Stochastic programming adds probability-modelled scenarios and recourse; robust optimisation adds protection against bounded ambiguity; distributionally robust methods add ambiguity over probability laws; rolling and online methods re-decide as state changes; and decision-focused learning trains predictive components against downstream loss. The evolved form selects among these mechanisms according to uncertainty type, consequence, recourse, observability, computational budget and evidence. Formal guarantees under a model do not establish that the model, ambiguity set or deployment loop fits reality. [S020–S033, S067–S069, S112, S119–S121]

## Citation-ready factual claims

| Claim | Durable source IDs |
| --- | --- |
| Early teletraffic theory treated calls, service capacity, loss and waiting as probabilistic operating phenomena rather than mere “noise”. | [S001, S002] |
| The 1913 Harris lot-size model formalised a setup/ordering versus holding-cost trade-off that later inventory theory generalised. | [S003] |
| Wartime operational research was multidisciplinary and mission-facing; post-war OR became a broad family rather than a single optimisation algorithm. | [S005, S006, S071, S072] |
| Linear programming makes represented scarcity, objectives and constraints explicit, but its optimum remains conditional on those inputs. | [S007] |
| Dynamic programming and Markov decision models distinguish a state-contingent policy from a fixed one-shot plan. | [S011, S012, S013] |
| Little’s law links average WIP, throughput and flow time under stated long-run conditions; it does not validate every queue model. | [S015] |
| Heavy-traffic and time-varying queue research shows why high utilisation and average-rate reasoning can coexist with severe delay. | [S016, S052, S053] |
| PERT and CPM arose as distinct project-network methods; later research adds resources, uncertainty and rolling execution. | [S018, S019, S060, S063] |
| Chance-constrained, stochastic, robust and distributionally robust optimisation answer different uncertainty questions and require different evidence. | [S020, S022, S025, S028, S029] |
| Decision analysis formalises alternatives, consequences, preferences and information value, while behavioural evidence limits claims that elicited preferences are descriptively stable. | [S038, S039, S043, S045, S046] |
| Multi-criteria rankings can depend on weights, measurement scale, normalisation and method choice; a scorecard does not remove judgement. | [S041, S078, S079, S080, S083] |
| Optimiser’s-curse analysis shows that selecting the estimated best alternative can create post-decision disappointment even before model-form error is considered. | [S070] |
| Simulation replications reduce sampling error, while input uncertainty and model-form validity require separate treatment. | [S084, S085, S086, S087, S088] |
| Forecast accuracy and operational decision value are not identical; decision-focused methods explicitly optimise downstream loss. | [S067, S068, S091, S092] |
| Deployed predictions can alter the population being predicted, creating endogenous feedback and drift. | [S096, S097] |
| Empirical proxy-bias evidence demonstrates that an apparently effective allocation score can encode a different outcome from the one stakeholders intend. | [S105] |
| Current OR literature still treats implementation feasibility, organisational relevance and the academic–practice gap as unresolved concerns. | [S101, S102] |
| Recent AI–OR work is framed as complementary and unfinished rather than as replacement of problem formulation, interpretability and human expertise. | [S103] |
| Modern maintenance optimisation extends age/replacement models toward condition information and coupled operations, while retaining failure-model and data burdens. | [S131, S132] |

## Evidence limits and claims not to make

- Do not claim that one formal methodology called “Evolved Decision and Operations Engineering” historically existed.
- Do not claim that solver optimality validates the objective, constraints, probabilities, alternatives or implementation.
- Do not claim that 100% utilisation, zero inventory, maximal parallelism or one universal reserve percentage is generally efficient.
- Do not claim that expected value, a weighted score, a critical path or a simulation is objectively authoritative without value and assumption ownership.
- Do not claim that more simulation runs reduce input or model-form uncertainty.
- Do not claim that DRO, DFL, RL, digital twins or predictive maintenance are mature universal endpoints; field and transfer evidence is uneven.
- Do not claim that a parametric queue or machine-scheduling model transfers to heterogeneous knowledge/agent work without empirical validation.
- Do not treat mathematical theorems under assumptions as empirical evidence that those assumptions hold.

## Direct lineage, convergence, and domain translation

| Class | Public distinction |
| --- | --- |
| Direct lineage | Documented queueing, inventory, OR, mathematical-programming, scheduling, simulation, decision-analysis, stochastic, robust and MCDA traditions. |
| Shared ancestry/import | Probability/statistics, utility/economics, control and systems analysis supplied formal structures but are not relabelled as OR-native. |
| Convergence | Implementation, fairness, proxy capture, model governance and problem structuring emerged across disciplines and criticism. |
| Domain translation | DFL, RL, AI–OR and learning-augmented algorithms instantiate older decision properties in new computational contexts. |
| Only analogous/unresolved | Knowledge and agent work may exhibit congestion and dependencies, but exact queue/scheduling formula transfer is not established. |

## Current-state and frontier notes

- Distributionally robust optimisation continues to develop statistical guarantees, multimodal and decision-dependent uncertainty, and learned ambiguity sets; calibration and external validity remain decisive. [S029, S120, S121]
- Decision-focused learning is maturing as a formal field, but feedback, distribution shift, prospective evaluation and deployment authority remain open. [S068, S069, S096, S097]
- Online and learning-augmented optimisation increasingly represents prediction error, switching cost and cross-level constraints instead of assuming perfect foresight. [S112, S119]
- Safe reinforcement-learning research still identifies safety, generalisation, scalability and constraint uncertainty as deployment limits. [S117]
- Queueing for modern compute and LLM systems is an active frontier with unresolved service, prediction and workload-abstraction questions. [S055, S113]
- Simulation research continues to emphasise input and parameter uncertainty, output analysis and simulation optimisation rather than raw run count. [S111]
- OR’s current professional discussion still emphasises problem formulation, implementation and human expertise alongside AI. [S101–S103]

## Freeze and packaging note

Research judgements, denominator and source identities were frozen before packaging. JSON generation performs syntax-only normalisation (UTF-8, deterministic key ordering/indentation and explicit arrays). The manifest records raw SHA-256 and byte count for substantive content members, a declared normalized self-hash for the manifest, and a declared normalized self-hash for the deterministic ZIP. Because neither a file nor an archive can contain its own raw cryptographic hash without changing, the user-facing outer receipt additionally supplies the raw manifest and raw ZIP hashes. This is an integrity-boundary disclosure, not a missing research artefact.
